parts.text:
1
Which estimate is reasonable?
A
1  10–3
kg for the mass of a grain of sand
B
1  10–2
m3 for the volume of a tennis ball
C
1  100
J for the work done lifting an apple from waist height to head height
D
1  104
W for the power of a light bulb in a house

hints: Compare $1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$ to a $1 \text{ g}$ paperclip and ask if a barely visible sand grain could have that mass.
Recall $W = mgh$ for the apple lift, using mass about $0.1 \text{ kg}$ and waist to head height about $0.5 \text{ m}$.
Check the tennis ball volume from radius about $0.035 \text{ m}$ and the house bulb power against the familiar $60 \text{ W}$ lamp versus $1 \times 10^{4} \text{ W}$.
walkthrough: List the four claimed orders of magnitude: $10^{-3} \text{ kg}$, $10^{-2} \text{ m}^{3}$, $10^{0} \text{ J}$, $10^{4} \text{ W}$, and test each against everyday sizes.
A sand grain is about $1 \text{ mm}$ across, so its mass is milligrams or less. $1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} = 1 \text{ g}$ is thousands of times too large.
A tennis ball has radius $r$ about $0.035 \text{ m}$, so $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ is about $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{3}$. $1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}^{3}$ is about 50 times too large.

For the apple, use $W = mgh$ with $m$ about $0.1 \text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $h$ about $0.5 \text{ m}$ from waist to head. $W$ is about $0.1 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 0.5 \text{ J}$, which has order of magnitude $1 \times 10^{0} \text{ J}$.
A house bulb is typically $5$ to $60 \text{ W}$. $1 \times 10^{4} \text{ W}$ is a factory load, not a bulb.
Only the apple work estimate matches its calculation. This is option C

A.explanation: $1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$ is $1 \text{ g}$, about a paperclip. A single grain of sand is far smaller, of order $10^{-6} \text{ kg}$.

B.explanation: $1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}^{3}$ is $10$ litres. A tennis ball of diameter about $7 \text{ cm}$ has volume of order $10^{-4} \text{ m}^{3}$.

C.explanation: For an apple of mass about $0.1 \text{ kg}$ lifted about $0.5 \text{ m}$, $W = mgh$ is about $0.5 \text{ J}$, of order $1 \times 10^{0} \text{ J}$.

D.explanation: $1 \times 10^{4} \text{ W}$ is $10 \text{ kW}$, like several electric heaters. A house light bulb is of order $10 \text{ W}$.
